newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Transport problems the focus of Central Asia summit.
newsitem.headline: Transport problems the focus of Central Asia summit.

text.p: The leaders of several Asian states met at a regional summit in Turkmenistan on Tuesday to examine ways of opening up resource-rich but landlocked Central Asia to world markets.

The heads of state of Turkey, Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan converged on the sleepy Turkmen capital Ashgabat for a meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) to review transport issues.
Pakistan's prime minister, Nawaz Sharif, was due to arrive later on Tuesday, while Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev sent a representative to the summit.
Ousted Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani also attended although the purist Islamic Taleban militia, which controls three-quarters of the war-ravaged country, was absent.
Plans to build pipelines to export massive amounts of oil and gas from the former Soviet states of Central Asia to the West are set to dominate discussions.

"Realisation of the pipeline networks, which is a vital project for the ECO region, will increase the welfare level of the peoples of the region," Turkish President Suleiman Demirel said in a speech, the text of which was made available to reporters.
The Central Asian states are desperate to break their almost total dependence on Russia for the export of their energy riches through Soviet-era pipelines.

Russia's tight grip on existing pipelines has severely restricted oil flows from Kazakhstan and brought Turkmenistan to its knees after Russia "diverted" Turkmen natural gas exports away from European clients with cash to impoverished former Soviet republics that cannot pay for them.
Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov, who welcomed the heads of state with an honour guard and brass bands, sounded an optimistic note about breaking Central Asia's transport deadlock.
"We must hail the fact that several of these new transport routes are already functioning," Niyazov said.
He added in a speech that $40-$50 billion needs to be invested in Central Asia's Russian export routes to the north and redirect communications to the south.
But diplomats say a new rail route south linking the Soviet-built rail network via Turkmenistan through diplomatically isolated Iran is barely functioning.
"There's very little moving on the Sarakhs rail link," said one diplomat based in the region.
An oil swaps deal between Iran and Kazakhstan, which could place up to six million tonnes of Kazakh crude on the Gulf, is stalled.
An ambitious plan to build a $2 billion gas pipeline south to Pakistan via Afghanistan is stalled by continued war.
While Niyazov called on participants not to "politicise" ECO, the war in Afghanistan looms very large over the summit.
An ambitious plan by U.S. Unocal Corp and Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil to build a $2 billion gas pipeline south to Pakistan via Afghanistan remains on the drawing board by the continued war.
Central Asian states fear the Taleban may launch a summer offensive, putting the militia right on their doorsteps.
